slides.title: Handhole, manhole or vault?
slides.sub: Same fiber network, three very different structures

slides.title: The name decides the cost and the safety rules.
slides.body: Whether a person climbs inside changes everything about the job.

slides.title: Handhole: work from above
slides.body: A shallow box, up to about 36 inches deep. Nobody enters. Splices, slack, drops and pull points. The cheapest option.

slides.title: Manhole: a person goes in
slides.body: An underground room with a ladder, where duct banks meet. In the US it is an OSHA permit-required confined space.

slides.title: The real cost of a manhole
slides.body: Gas testing, forced ventilation, an attendant at the surface and a rescue plan, all before anyone climbs down.

slides.title: Vault: room for equipment
slides.body: Larger chambers for splitters or building entrances. Common where above-ground cabinets are not allowed.

slides.title: Use the smallest that works
items: India says chamber, Australia says pit

caption:
Handhole, manhole and vault get used like they mean the same thing. They don't.

A handhole is worked from the surface. A manhole is a room a person climbs into, with confined-space rules attached. A vault holds equipment. Swipe for where each one belongs.
